description:
Orbit Sync is a passionate team leveraging satellite data to bridge MODIS and VIIRS active fire observations. By harmonizing hotspot data and visualizing fire patterns, we aim to enhance wildfire monitoring, environmental awareness, and informed decision-making.

Our motto: Bridging Satellites, Connecting Fire Insights.
summary:
OrbitSync – Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS Active Fire Data

We developed FlareFusion, a web-based platform that harmonizes NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active fire hotspot data to enable more consistent and reliable fire activity analysis. The platform addresses differences in spatial resolution and detection characteristics between the two satellite sensors using spatial-temporal matching and robust regression-based harmonization to convert MODIS observations into a VIIRS-equivalent representation.

It provides interactive maps, a burning activity calendar, cross-sensor comparisons, historical trends, statistical analytics, and machine learning-based anomaly detection. Users can explore fire activity across different regions and time periods while retaining sensor provenance and understanding the differences between raw and harmonized observations.

This project is important because inconsistent satellite measurements can make long-term fire comparisons challenging. By improving cross-sensor consistency, OrbitSync supports researchers, environmental agencies, disaster management teams, and policymakers in monitoring fire patterns, identifying unusual activity, and making better-informed decisions for wildfire management and environmental protection.
details:
Pyronix is a web app that combines MODIS and VIIRS fire hotspots into a single burning activity calendar for any selected area. It uses NASA FIRMS data (MODIS, VIIRS SNPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) with Natural Earth boundaries, and presents everything on the VIIRS scale so fire activity from both satellites can be viewed together.

Benefits: It gives one consistent fire record across satellites, avoids duplicate counting, and shows fire seasons in a calendar anyone can read. Users can also export results as CSV or GeoJSON for their own analysis.

Impact: It makes satellite fire data easier to use for understanding fire seasons, planning burn and prevention periods, and supporting climate and air-quality research.

Tools: NASA FIRMS data and Natural Earth boundaries. A Python pipeline handles four stages: aggregation, harmonization, building and forecasting. It uses Scikit-learn, Pandas and NumPy for machine learning. The backend is Flask REST APIs, and the frontend is React with Leaflet for interactive maps and analytics.

Creativity: It turns complex satellite data into a simple, visual calendar. It also adds forecasting, so users can see likely fire activity ahead, not just past records.

Factors considered: Differences between the satellites, overlapping detections of the same fire, ease of use for non-experts, a modular pipeline that is easy to debug, and open export formats for wider reuse.
